 CORE
August 20, 2025

Highlight
Show highlights
FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Review the epidemiology, etiology, and pathoanatomy of clubfoot.
Perform an appropriate evaluation of a patient in whom clubfoot is suspected.
Describe the nonsurgical management of clubfoot via the Ponseti method.
Describe the surgical management of clubfoot refractory to cast immobilization.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
The four basic component deformities in a patient with clubfoot are cavus, adductus, varus,
and equinus.
Forefoot adductus results from medial and plantar subluxation of the navicular bone on the
talar head.
The hindfoot is adducted and inverted into varus under the talus.

The entire foot appears supinated; however, the forefoot is pronated relative to the hindfoot,
leading to the cavus deformity.
The muscles and tendons of the gastrocnemius-soleus complex, the posterior tibialis, and the
long toe flexors are shortened (Resources 1 and 2).
Overview
Clubfoot is a congenital foot deformity consisting of hindfoot equinus and varus and midfoot
and forefoot adduction and cavus.
Potential etiologies include abnormal fibrosis, neurologic abnormalities, and arrested
embryologic development. Intrauterine positioning is not a factor (sufficient room is present in
the uterus in the first trimester, the time during which clubfoot forms).
Epidemiology
1:1,000 in general population (6.8 per 1,000 in Polynesian population)
2:1 ratio in males versus females
One-half of cases are bilateral.
24.4% of individuals with clubfoot have a family history of idiopathic clubfoot.1
Anatomy and Biomechanics

Anatomy and Biomechanics
The anatomy of a clubfoot affects the bones, tendons, ligaments, joint capsules, and
neurovascular structures. Although the various deformities generally can be corrected
via serial cast immobilization using the Ponseti method (with or without the addition of
some surgical procedures), persistent histologic and morphologic differences are
present in a clubfoot compared with an unaffected foot.
Clinical pearls about clubfoot anatomy—Families should be educated about some of the
temporary and permanent findings early in the course of clubfoot management to
establish appropriate expectations. Examples of temporary anatomic changes families
will notice during the course of Ponseti treatment include the following:

Deep creases appear on the lateral sinus tarsi area as the foot is gradually corrected
via cast immobilization. Excess skin is present on the stretched out lateral foot that
becomes redundant as the foot is derotated; these folds of skin may look like cuts, so
reassurance about the temporary nature of the skin folds is helpful.
As the foot is derotated 60° to 70° externally with serial cast immobilization (and then
held in external rotation via post-casting braces), many families worry that the feet will
turn out permanently; therefore, reassurance about the foot progression angle
correcting over time and with ambulation helps guide parents’ expectations.
Permanent calf girth and foot/shoe size differences can be expected in patients with
unilateral clubfoot.
Osteology
Morphologic changes are observed as early as the second trimester in fetuses with clubfoot.
Midfoot adductus results from a navicular that is displaced medially and articulates with the
medial talar head (and almost touches the medial malleolus).
The hindfoot varus deformity is because of a flexed, medially bowed, inverted calcaneus that is
adducted under the talus.
The talus is in equinus; a short talar neck and medial/plantar deviation of the talar head are
present.
Cuneiforms and metatarsals are normally shaped but adducted. Cavus results from a first
metatarsal that is more plantar flexed than the lateral metatarsals (midfoot pronation)..2,3
Vascular Anatomy
Clubfoot often is associated with absence or hypoplasia of the anterior tibial artery. Whether
vascular dysplasia is causative or associated remains unclear.4
Nerves
Clubfoot may be the result of a (regional) primary nerve abnormality as evidenced by an
increase in the ration of type I:II muscle fibers.5

Tendons
No histologic differences exist compared with non-clubfoot tendons.
The tibialis posterior tendon and sheath are grossly hypertrophied/enlarged, especially near
its insertion.
Tendons of the tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus, and extensor hallucis longus are
displaced medially.6
Joints and Ligaments
The medial/posterior joint capsules and the medial/posterior tarsal ligaments (such as the
medial talocalcaneal ligament and the inferior tibiofibular syndesmosis) are thickened, fibrotic,
and contracted.
The posterior tibiotalar, fibulotalar, and fibulocalcaneal ligaments are thick, short, and matted
with fibrous tissue and occasionally are pulled into the posterior joint.
Contracture of the deltoid ligament holds the calcaneus inverted.
The tibionavicular and plantar calcaneonavicular ligaments hold the navicular medially
displaced (along with the posterior tibial tendon).2,3
Musculature
Histologically, increased fibrosis of muscle tissue is present in clubfeet (normal muscle fibers
are present, but more intercellular connective tissue is present).3
Grossly, the gastrocnemius, soleus, and posterior tibialis are smaller and shorter in clubfeet
than normal feet.
An anomalous flexor muscle of the calf is present in some patients with clubfoot.7
Etiology
Unknown and likely multifactorial
Possibly abnormal muscle fibrosis, neurologic abnormality, arrest of embryonic development
Genetic component in at least some patients (heterogeneous, multiple genes, other
environmental factors involved)
PITX1 and TBX4 (possible hindlimb development pathway genes) are involved in etiology of
clubfoot.8,9

Natural History
Not a painful condition, but if left unmanaged, the contractures will not resolve on their own.
Patients with clubfoot will walk on the lateral/dorsal foot, and permanent deformities will be
present, making shoe wear difficult; ambulation eventually will be painful.
Risk Factors
Unaffected parents with an affected child have a 2.5% to 6.5% risk of having another child with
clubfoot.
Early amniocentesis (before 11 weeks gestation) is associated with a higher risk of clubfoot.
Classification
The Diméglio-Bensahel (Diméglio score) and Catterall-Pirani (Pirani score) classification
systems are based on the severity of the clinical findings and the correctability of the
deformity.
The Diméglio score is out of 20 points (higher score is more severe). The system assigns 1 to
4 points for each of four deformity planes (equinus, varus, derotation, and adductus) and
assigns 1 additional point for the presence of a posterior crease, a medial crease, cavus, or
poor muscle condition. The total number of points out of 20 determines if the foot is benign,
moderate, severe, or very severe (Figure 1).

Figure 1 Illustrations show the Diméglio score for clubfoot. Each major component of
clubfoot (equinus [top left], varus [top right], rotation [bottom left], adduction [bottom
right]) is graded from 0 to 4 points. Additional points are added for a deep posterior crease
(1 point), a deep medial crease (1 point), cavus (1 point), and muscle abnormalities (1 point).
The sum of these parameters constitutes a total on a 20-point scale, in which a higher score
indicates more severe deformity. Clubfoot is classified as benign (<6 points), moderate (6 to
10 points), severe (11 to 15 points), or very severe (>15 points). (Reproduced with permission
from Lampasi M, Abati CN, Bettuzzi C, Stilli S, Trisolino G: Comparison of Dimeglio and Pirani
score in predicting number of casts and need for tenotomy in clubfoot correction using the
Ponseti method. Int Orthop 2018;42[10]:2429-2436.)

Figure 2 Illustrations show the Pirani score for clubfoot. Each item is given a score of 0 (no

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Common clinical findings are a small foot, a small calf, a slightly shortened tibia, and skin
creases medially and posteriorly.
Clubfeet associated with arthrogryposis, myelomeningocele, diastrophic dysplasia, and
amniotic band syndrome are more challenging to manage and more prone to relapse.
Radiographic parameters correlate with Diméglio scores; therefore, radiographs generally are
not obtained during the initial treatment course to avoid radiation exposure.10
On AP and lateral radiographs of a clubfoot, the talus and calcaneus are less divergent and
more parallel (smaller talocalcaneal angle) than normal.
Patient History
Diagnosed via ultrasonography prenatally beginning in the second trimester (may result in a
false-positive rate as high as 25%) or clinically at birth
History of other family members with clubfoot also is relevant.

Physical Examination
Clubfeet have a distinct clinical appearance: cavus/adduction of the forefoot and
varus/equinus of the hindfoot (Figure 3).
Equinus that cannot be passively corrected above 90° is the most diagnostic aspect of the
physical examination. Many newborn babies have varying degrees of adductus, inversion, and
internal rotation of one or both feet secondary to intrauterine positioning; however, tightness
in these planes may be indicative of clubfoot if rigid equinus also is present.
Position of the clubfoot is examined, and the presence of cavus, adductus, varus, and equinus
of varying tightness can be ascertained and quantified/measured on physical examination.
The rest of the baby also should be examined, assessing for any concurrent upper extremity
contractures, spine abnormalities, or skin abnormalities, which may help recognize non-
idiopathic or syndromic clubfeet.
Figure 3 Clinical photograph of the lower extremities of an infant with idiopathic clubfoot shows
the characteristic deformities of cavus, metatarsus adductus, hindfoot varus, and equinus.
(Reproduced from Nemeth BA, Noonan KJ: Treatment of clubfoot using the Ponseti method, in
Colvin AC, Flatow E, eds: Atlas of Essential Orthopaedic Procedures, ed 2. Rosemont, IL, American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 950-956.)
SEND FEEDBACK

Neurovascular Examination
In patients with idiopathic clubfoot, sensation generally is normal.
In patients with spina bifida–associated clubfoot, sensation is diminished based on neurologic
level (this predisposes patients in this population to a higher risk of skin breakdown with
cast/brace immobilization).
Motor function is difficult to determine because of limitation of full motion by contractures
and limitations in examining neonates.
Absence of toe dorsiflexion with plantar stimulation of the feet and a resting position in
plantar flexion (drop toe sign) may indicate a neurologic etiology of the clubfoot.11
Anterior tibial artery hypoplasia/absence is common; therefore, a palpable dorsalis pedis pulse
may not be present in this location.
Imaging Studies
Plain radiographs are of limited use during the neonatal period and are not routinely obtained
unless associated limb deformities are noted during physical examination.
The talus and calcaneus are less divergent/more parallel on AP and lateral radiographs of a
clubfoot compared with a normal foot.
CT/MRI/ultrasonography are not routinely performed in initial diagnosis/management of
clubfoot.
Differential Diagnosis
Several foot deformities are present at birth that initially may be referred for orthopaedic
evaluation of clubfoot. The appearances of these diagnoses, such as calcaneovalgus foot and
rocker-bottom deformity/congenital vertical talus, can be made clinically (and confirmed via
plain radiographs if necessary). These are different conditions and have different prognoses,
natural histories, and treatment courses than clubfoot.
The differential diagnosis for idiopathic clubfoot includes syndromic/non-idiopathic clubfoot
(in which the associated syndrome or condition may not be clinically evident prenatally or
immediately at birth).
Tibial deficiency (or another limb deficiency)
Amniotic band/Streeter dysplasia
Myelodysplasia, caudal regression
Multiple contracture syndromes, such as amyoplasia/arthrogryposis

Management
Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical management (Ponseti technique) should be the main treatment option. Reserving
extensive surgical releases for refractory cases or teratologic clubfeet prevents late stiffness
and pain later in life.
Indications
Nonsurgical Ponseti cast immobilization (or stretching/French functional method) should be
considered in almost all clubfeet (idiopathic or syndromic). Nonsurgical treatment of patients
of any age who have clubfoot can be attempted; however, the ideal age for initiation of the
Ponseti method remains unknown. General treatment timing guidelines include the following:
Serial cast immobilization initiated in infants aged at least 1 to 3 months results in a lower
rate of relapse and better clinical outcomes than treatment initiated in infants younger than
1 month.10
No difference exists in the number of casts necessary to achieve full correction, the need for
tenotomy, recurrence rates, and the eventual need for tibialis anterior tendon transfer in
infants older or younger than 6 months who undergo serial cast immobilization.13
Similar outcomes are observed in full-term infants treated via serial clubfoot cast
immobilization and preterm infants in whom treatment is delayed until they reach full
gestational age.14
Contraindications
Foot too small to be casted or braced (prematurity)
Unsafe to initiate serial cast immobilization immediately (because of other health issues, such
as skin fragility, large fluid shifts, or vascular/perfusion compromise)
Techniques/Procedures
Ponseti method2,15 (Resource 3)
The outcome is much better than with historic cast immobilization techniques (80% to 90%
success rate versus 10% to 50%, respectively).

Video 1 Nogueira MP: What can go wrong and what to do about it? from Mosca VS, mod:
Advanced Ponseti course and minimally invasive management of vertical talus. Presented at
the Annual Meeting of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, San Diego, CA,

Long leg casts are changed weekly. Long leg casts are imperative because they stay on a
small baby leg much better than a short below-knee cast and because long leg casts provide
rotational control of the correction that a short leg cast cannot.
The initial cast places the forefoot in supination to correct forefoot cavus.
Counterpressure is applied to the lateral aspect of the talar head only; it is not applied to the
calcaneus.
Percutaneous Achilles tenotomy frequently is required before final cast application to
manage residual equinus (as many as 90% of feet; Figure 5; Video 2).
The technique for performing the tenotomy varies based on surgeon preference.
Occasionally, the procedure is performed (in young infants younger than 3 to 4 months) in
a clinic setting with the use of local anesthetic agent (topical lidocaine/prilocaine cream
and/or subcutaneous injection of local anesthetic); other times, the procedure is performed
(in older infants or for repeat tenotomy) in the operating room with the use of a general
anesthetic agent.
The baby is placed in the supine position, with an assistant holding the foot in maximum
dorsiflexion so the Achilles tendon is taut. A small blade (ophthalmic blade or No. 15 blade)
is then inserted on the medial side of the tendon approximately 1 cm above the tendon

released percutaneously, stopping short of the skin before removing the blade through the
same incision. A palpable release/increase in dorsiflexion should occur, with the goal being
at least 10° of dorsiflexion.
A long leg Ponseti cast is applied with the foot in maximum correction and left in place for 3
weeks before switching to an abduction foot orthosis.

alternative technique, the blade is inserted at a 45° angle to the skin. The handle is then

Foot abduction orthoses (Denis-Brown or John Mitchell boots and bar) are used to prevent
recurrence (Figure 6). The ideal position of the shoes is shoulder-width apart on the bar
with the affected foot/feet externally rotated 60° and unaffected foot externally rotated
30°. The recommended use is 23 hours per day for a minimum of 3 months after cast
immobilization and then during naps and overnight until at least age 4 years.
Recurrences typically are managed via repeat manipulation and cast immobilization
followed by resumption of brace management.
Tibialis anterior tendon transfer may be required in patients with dynamic swing-phase
supination. If indicated, this procedure typically is performed between age 3 and 5 years
(Video 3).

Daily manipulations are required for clubfeet in newborns, typically performed and directed
by a physical therapist.
The feet are taped, not casted, in position after manipulations.
Continuous passive motion devices are used for the first 12 weeks of management.
Physical therapy sessions are continued until the child is walking or the deformity is stable.
Surgical Management
Surgical management is reserved for feet refractory to manipulations/cast immobilization,
syndrome-associated clubfoot, and delayed presentation (children older than 1 to 2 years).
The surgical plan should be individualized for each patient. Releases of the posteromedial
structures are performed as necessary (the a la carte approach).
Residual deformities may require surgical management (Table 1).
Tibialis anterior tendon transfer (from the base of the first metatarsal usually to the lateral
cuneiform) is necessary in approximately one-third of patients treated via the Ponseti method
because of recurrence secondary to dynamic foot supination during the swing phase of gait.

Indications
Clubfeet refractory to manipulation or cast immobilization
Clubfeet with muscle imbalances, even after deformity correction, such as tibialis anterior
overpull into supination
Contraindications
Extensive posteromedial surgical release should not be the first line of management if serial
cast immobilization has not been attempted. Surgical release causes scarring and stiffness in
the long-term follow-up of patients with clubfoot.16
Techniques/Procedures
Posteromedial release for teratogenic clubfoot (associated with syndromes such as
myelodysplasia, arthrogryposis, and diastrophic dysplasia)
The individual components of the posteromedial release can be performed a la carte for
certain deformities refractory to cast immobilization alone.
Tibialis anterior tendon transfer for dynamic supination
Numerous techniques have been described for surgical release of clubfoot deformities
refractory to cast immobilization or recurrent deformities or muscle imbalances. Percutaneous
Achilles tenotomy technique was discussed as part of the Ponseti method; therefore, the main
techniques are:
Posteromedial Release
Preoperative planning
Thorough physical examination with attention paid to the direction and extent of the
deformity
Patient positioning
Prone position, with a rolled-up towel under the anterior ankle to allow for full dorsiflexion if
it can be achieved

A thigh tourniquet can be placed but may be left uninflated to allow for palpation or Doppler
assessment of pulse while working near/protecting the neurovascular bundle.
Patient positioned near the foot end of the bed so the surgeon can work from the end of the
bed
Surgical approaches
Make a Cincinnati (transverse) incision 1 cm above the posterior heel crease (this extends
from just below the lateral tip of fibula to just below the medial malleolus and out onto the
medial foot by the cuneiform if necessary).
Release the Achilles tendon (Z-lengthening in idiopathic clubfeet and tendonectomy in
teratologic clubfeet).
Identify and protect the neurovascular bundle with the use of a vessel loop.
Start releasing only structures that are contracted after cast immobilization posterolaterally,
then posteromedially, and finally plantarmedially if necessary.
Posterolateral structures: calcaneofibular ligament, part of the peroneal tendon sheath,
tibiotalar joint to the lateral dome of the talus down to the distal talofibular ligament
Posteromedial structures: Z-lengthen flexor hallucis longus, which is identified by having
the most distal muscle belly; posterior facet of the subtalar joint; tibiotalar joint to the
medial dome of the talus down to the deltoid ligament
Plantarmedial structures: three abductor hallucis origins, plantar fascia, flexor digitorum
brevis, Z-lengthen the posterior tibialis tendon, talonavicular joint capsule, spring ligament
(Figure 7).

Postoperative management
The long-leg cast is left in place for 3 to 4 weeks postoperatively, after which it is changed to
boot and bar braces (or another type of brace, such as an ankle-foot orthosis).
Pitfalls and preventative measures
Skin healing/tension/slough (prevent via pie-crusting or cast immobilization initially in a
partially corrected position and return to operating room 1 or 2 weeks later for a cast
change into fully corrected position)
Damage to the neurovascular structures (avoid by identifying and protecting and by
ensuring good perfusion to skin edges and toes with the foot in a fully corrected position

21/29

before cast immobilization)
Clubfoot recurrence (avoid by releasing structures until correction is complete and via
postoperative immobilization/bracing)
Tibialis Anterior Tendon Transfer
Preoperative planning
Physical examination of the walking child may show isolated dynamic supination in which the
patient does not have any fixed recurrence/clubfoot deformity but demonstrates rotation of
the forefoot into supination during the swing phase of gait, which affects the lateral border
of the foot at heel strike. The patient also may have concurrent static clubfoot deformity
(recurrence of equinus, varus, adductus, or cavus) in addition to dynamic supination.
Preoperative plan should include repeat serial cast immobilization for any clubfoot
recurrence before tibialis anterior tendon transfer. The tendon transfer cannot correct
deformity; it can only correct muscle imbalance.
If the patient is 3 years or younger, plain radiographs may help determine if the ossification
center of the lateral cuneiform is present and able to accept a tunnel of approximately 4 to 5
mm for anchoring the tendon transfer.
Patient positioning
Supine position; can use thigh tourniquet; position patient near the foot end of the bed
Surgical approaches
Perform Z-lengthening of the Achilles tendon if the patient cannot dorsiflex 10° beyond
neutral.
Make a dorsomedial foot incision (centered over the palpable anterior tibialis tendon)
extending from just distal to the ankle crease to near the base of the first metatarsal. Release
the tibialis anterior tendon from its insertion on the first metatarsal base and make a Bunnell
stitch in the distal 1 cm of the tendon.
Make a dorsolateral foot incision using the interval between extensor digitorum longus
(small toe) and the peroneus tertius. Use fluoroscopy with the foot in internal rotation,
oblique position, so all the cuneiforms are not overlapping, and place a Keith needle in the
center of the lateral cuneiform (Figure 8).
Make a cruciate incision in the dorsal periosteum, and use a Freer elevator to raise the
periosteum; then drill with the use of an approximately 4-mm drill through the lateral
cuneiform from dorsolateral to plantarmedial.

Postoperative management
A long leg cast with the foot in the corrected position and non–weight bearing are
recommended for at least 4 weeks postoperatively. The plantar button is removed 4 weeks
postoperatively. Various postoperative protocols exist for advancement of weight bearing
(usually 4 to 6 weeks postoperatively) and immobilization (in long or short leg cast for a total
of 4 to 6 weeks postoperatively) and bracing (none versus ankle-foot orthosis versus boots
and bar).
Pitfalls and preventative measures
Pressure sore from plantar button (avoid by applying sterile felt to disperse pressure over a
wider area or by using other fixation methods for the tendon transfer)
Weakness of the transferred tendon (avoid by ensuring any clubfoot recurrence/equinus is
corrected before tendon transfer and via adequate fixation of tendon/immobilization to
prevent pull-out of the tendon).
Complications
Recurrence
Reported rates of clubfoot recurrence are highly variable (2% to 45%) and usually evident by
age 4 years. Recurrence commonly requires repeat cast immobilization, bracing, and
occasionally a la carte surgical releases.17,18 Noncompliance with post-casting brace use is the
most common risk factor for recurrence; however, recurrence can occur despite strict
adherence to the bracing protocol.
Soft-Tissue Reaction
Skin complications from cast immobilization can be minimized by avoiding excess padding or
layers of cast material, keeping cast edges dry, and avoiding pressing too hard in any one place
during cast molding. Patients with an insensate clubfoot (amniotic bands, spina bifida) have a
higher risk for cast/soft-tissue complications.

Avoidance of intra-articular surgical clubfoot releases is the best method to prevent long-term

Neural Injury/Nerve Palsy
Not common with cast immobilization for clubfoot but may result if neural structures are not
protected during surgical releases
Dorsal Bunion
This deformity occurs after the surgical management of clubfeet. It results from elevation of
the first metatarsal because of the unopposed pull of the tibialis anterior tendon secondary to
inadvertent transection of the peroneus longus tendon. This is accompanied by plantar flexion
across the metatarsophalangeal joint of the hallux because of residual or recurrent tightness
of the flexor tendons of the great toe. This combination of deformities creates the
characteristic dorsal bunion deformity.

At least 5-year follow-up after clubfoot management via the Ponseti method19
37% of patients adhered to the bracing protocol.
68% of patients had 1 or more relapses.
38% of patients underwent tendon transfer.
62% of patients had good outcomes, 38% of patients had fair outcomes, and no patients had
poor outcomes.
Follow-up after clubfoot management via extensive soft-tissue releases showed that stiff,
